title: The Benjamin Franklin Effect
description: When you do a favor for someone, your brain unconsciously resolves the inconsistency by convincing itself that you must like them.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: When you do a favor for someone, your brain unconsciously resolves the inconsistency (“Why am I helping them?”) by convincing itself that you must like them. Liking grows from action, not the other way around.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A coworker who initially found you annoying starts warming up after you ask them for a small, genuine favor (borrowing a charger, getting their opinion on something).
After you lend a book to an acquaintance, you feel a surprising sense of investment in that person.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: They voluntarily offer more help later.
They initiate casual conversation more frequently.
They defend or speak positively about you to others afterward.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “Let me know if you need anything else.”
“I think I was wrong about them; they’re actually pretty decent.”

sections.title: Warning Signs (of someone engineering it)
content: A person repeatedly asks for tiny, easy favors early in a relationship.
They seem overly appreciative to lock in the effect.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Cognitive dissonance: the brain dislikes contradiction between action (helping) and belief (indifference). To reduce discomfort, it alters the belief. This was validated in Jecker & Landy (1969) and replicated many times.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Notice if you’re being nudged to grant favors by someone who previously showed no interest.
Separate your evaluation of the person from the act of helping.
Ask: “Would I still help if I didn’t think I had to like them afterward?”

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking that doing someone a favor will always make them like you. The effect mainly operates on the helper’s own feelings.
Refusing to ask for help to avoid being a burden, missing a powerful bonding mechanism.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: You join a new team and one senior member seems cold. Instead of avoiding them, you ask for a small piece of advice on a project. They oblige. Over the next week, they start greeting you warmly, ask about your weekend, and eventually become an ally. The shift started with that tiny request.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The fastest way to get someone to like you is sometimes to ask them for something small, not to give them something.
